title: The pool filled in
hookLine: invaders filled the Harmandir's pool with rubbish, and Sikhs vowed to restore it

cards: The water comes first. At the Harmandir there's a wide pool, still and bright, with the temple sitting in the middle of it and its reflection beneath. People walk all the way around; some bathe at the steps.

The whole place is built around that water. Now take the water away. Tradition says that when Abdali's commanders held Amritsar, they had the pool filled in with rubbish, earth and filth, and the sacred place was defiled.
A messenger rides south with the news.

teach.h: THE POOL IS THE GURUS' OWN WORK.
teach.b: Start with what the pool is. Tradition says Guru Ram Das began digging it, and Guru Arjan finished the work and built the Harmandir in its center.
Tradition also says the city took its name from it: Amritsar, the pool of amrit, the water of immortality. And Guru Arjan sang about it.

In a hymn in the Granth, in paraphrase, he says that God himself stood up to finish the work of his saints, and that the land is lovely and the pool is lovely, filled with nectar-water. So the pool isn't decoration.
In Sikh memory it's the Gurus' own work, made by hand and blessed in song.

teach.h: FILLED IN TO SAY: THIS IS OVER.
teach.b: Tradition reads the filling as a message: this is over. The Sikh answer was a vow.
Tradition says that when the news reached Damdama, Baba Deep Singh, yesterday's old scholar, swore to free the Harmandir, and set out.

teach.h: KAR SEVA: ONE BASKET AT A TIME.
teach.b: Leave the ride for another time; stay with what came after the vow. Restoring a pool isn't one dramatic act. It's baskets.

People standing in mud, passing rubble hand to hand, carrying it out, again and again, until the water can come back. Sikhs call that shared physical work for the Guru's house kar seva, the service of the hands.

And Sikhs tell of the pool being cleaned by kar seva in later times too, with ordinary people, young and old, carrying out silt in baskets. The vow and the basket belong together. One says it will be made right.
The other makes it right, one load at a time.

how: Sikhs walk around the sarovar at the Harmandir Sahib and some bathe at its steps, and the pool has been cleaned in later times by kar seva, with volunteers carrying out silt by hand.

o: the river by Amritsar where pilgrims go to bathe
the golden dome that sits on top of the Harmandir
the sacred pool, like the one around the Harmandir

games.q: you're a Sikh far from Amritsar. a rider brings news: the pool at the Harmandir has been filled with rubbish. what do you do?
o: vow to restore it, and go.
wait for someone else to deal with it.
games.why: tradition says Baba Deep Singh vowed to free the Harmandir and set out, and the pool was later restored by hand, basket by basket.

practice: Look around and choose one small patch that's been let go, a corner of a desk, a shelf, a folder on your screen, and clear just that, slowly, one thing at a time, the way you'd carry one basket. If you can't move, picture it.
When it's clear, look at it for one breath, and if you pray, say Waheguru as you finish.

wordCard.voice: sarovar, the sacred pool. Tradition says invaders filled the one at the Harmandir with rubbish, and Sikhs vowed to restore it, with a vow and then with baskets. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sarovar, a pool or tank; the sacred pool around the Harmandir Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: restore it. Big repairs are made of small loads, carried one at a time. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: The defiling of the sarovar and Baba Deep Singh's vow, Sikh tradition
